Global electric vehicle sales topped 20 million units in 2025, with battery innovations like sodium-ion tech accelerating adoption across sectors. Companies such as CATL now push sodium-ion batteries into passenger cars, trucks, and storage systems, complementing lithium-ion dominance. For instance, these batteries cut reliance on scarce lithium while matching performance in harsh climates. Electric vehicle applications benefit hugely, from urban delivery vans to long-range sedans. Moreover, lower production costs make them ideal for mass-market growth.

## Sodium-Ion Tech Hits Commercial Scale

CATL announced at its December 2025 supplier conference plans for widespread sodium-ion battery rollout in 2026. The Naxtra brand targets battery swaps, passenger vehicles, commercial trucks, and energy storage. Analysts note this shift from early trials to full deployment, with prices staying far below lithium-ion equivalents. Consequently, fleets gain affordable options for electrification. Electric vehicle applications expand rapidly here, as sodium-ion cells handle real-world demands effectively.

## Naxtra Brand Delivers Key Specs

CATL launched Naxtra in April 2025, kicking off mass production of sodium-ion cells. These operate from -40°C to 70°C, perfect for extreme weather. Formats include passenger power packs and 24V truck solutions. Next-gen versions hit 175 Wh/kg energy density, enabling over 500km pure-electric range. Therefore, drivers enjoy reliable performance without range anxiety. Electric vehicle applications shine in cold regions, where lithium-ion often falters.

## Safety Certifications Lead the Pack

CATL’s sodium-ion batteries passed China’s strict GB 38031-2025 standard first. This covers thermal stability, impact resistance, and fast-charging cycles, effective mid-2026. Third-party tests confirmed packs meet all criteria. As a result, regulators greenlight them for traction use. Compared to lithium-ion, they offer better safety and lower emissions. Thus, electric vehicle applications in safety-critical fleets become viable sooner.

## Performance Edges Over Lithium-Ion

Sodium-ion excels in low temperatures, retaining charge where rivals drop off. It supports extended ranges and reduces carbon footprints by using abundant sodium. CATL pairs it with lithium-ion in a “dual-star” strategy for 2026. Industry forecasts predict sodium-ion market booms through 2030, especially in storage and low-speed EVs. Furthermore, this eases supply chain pressures. Electric vehicle applications diversify, from city buses to grid backups.

Policies in China back this tech via national strategies for new energy vehicles. CATL aligns production with customer timelines, ensuring supply matches demand. Consequently, manufacturers integrate sodium-ion faster into hybrids and full EVs. Global players watch closely, as cost drops spur competition. Electric vehicle applications transform logistics and public transit. Overall, 2026 marks a pivot toward hybrid battery chemistries, boosting sustainability and affordability.

## Why CATL's Sodium-Ion Battery Matters for 2026 EV Buyers

For years, the EV battery conversation has centered on two lithium-ion chemistries: NMC (nickel manganese cobalt) and LFP (lithium iron phosphate). In 2026, a third option is entering mass production — CATL's sodium-ion battery, first previewed in 2021 and now reaching commercial-scale deployment in select Chinese-market vehicles and energy storage systems. If you've been searching for CATL sodium-ion battery availability 2026, the short answer is: it's here in limited applications, but not yet in most EVs sold in the United States.

This guide breaks down what sodium-ion technology actually offers, how it compares to the LFP and NMC packs already in millions of EVs on the road, and what current battery ownership really looks like — from degradation curves and warranty coverage to replacement costs and health-monitoring best practices.

## CATL Sodium-Ion Batteries: 2026 Availability and What They Offer

CATL (Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. Limited), the world's largest EV battery manufacturer, announced its first-generation sodium-ion cell in July 2021 with an energy density of 160 Wh/kg at the cell level. By 2026, CATL has scaled production and begun integrating sodium-ion packs into budget-oriented EVs — primarily through its partnership with Chery Automobile in China, where the technology targets the sub-¥100,000 (roughly $14,000) micro-EV and city-car segment.

Key specs of CATL's Gen-1 sodium-ion cell (2026 production):

* Energy density: ~160 Wh/kg (cell-level), compared to ~170-200 Wh/kg for LFP and ~250-300 Wh/kg for NMC
* Cold-weather performance: Retains over 90% capacity at -20°C (-4°F), significantly outperforming both LFP and NMC in freezing conditions
* Fast-charge capability: 10-80% in approximately 15 minutes under optimal thermal conditions
* Thermal stability: Superior to NMC; passes nail-penetration tests without thermal runaway
* Raw material advantage: Sodium is roughly 400x more abundant than lithium, eliminating dependence on lithium, cobalt, and nickel supply chains

The trade-off is energy density. A sodium-ion pack delivering the same range as a 60 kWh LFP pack would weigh approximately 15-25% more, making it best suited for compact and city EVs rather than long-range sedans or large SUVs. For US buyers, sodium-ion availability in 2026 is effectively zero in domestically sold vehicles — CATL's US-market footprint remains constrained by IRS §30D battery-sourcing requirements that exclude batteries with components from certain foreign entities of concern (FEOC), and CATL qualifies as such under current rules.

## Battery Chemistry Showdown: LFP vs NMC vs Sodium-Ion

Understanding which chemistry powers your EV matters for range, longevity, charging behavior, and cold-weather usability. Here's how the three primary chemistries compare as of 2026:

| Attribute | NMC/NCA (Nickel-based) | LFP (Lithium Iron Phosphate) | Sodium-Ion (CATL Gen-1) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Energy density (cell-level) | 250–300 Wh/kg | 170–200 Wh/kg | ~160 Wh/kg |
| Cycle life (to 80% capacity) | 1,000–2,000 cycles | 3,000–5,000+ cycles | ~3,000+ cycles (estimated) |
| Cold performance (-20°C) | ~60–70% retention | ~50–60% retention | ~90%+ retention |
| Cost per kWh (pack-level, 2026) | $120–$145 | $80–$100 | $60–$80 (projected at scale) |
| Thermal stability | Moderate (requires BMS) | High | Very high |
| State-of-charge estimation | Linear voltage curve (easy) | Flat voltage curve (harder) | Moderate (steeper than LFP) |
| Typical EV applications | Long-range, performance | Standard-range, fleet, daily | Budget city EVs, storage |
| Key raw materials | Lithium, nickel, cobalt, manganese | Lithium, iron, phosphate | Sodium, iron, manganese |

LFP vs NMC — which is better? There's no universal winner. NMC delivers the highest energy density, making it the default for long-range vehicles like the Tesla Model S, Hyundai Ioniq 6 Long Range, and BMW iX. If you need 300+ miles of EPA range in a midsize sedan, NMC is still the practical choice. LFP sacrifices some range per kilogram but wins on cycle life (often 3-5x longer), cost, and thermal safety — which is why Tesla uses LFP in the Model 3 and Model Y Standard Range trims, and Ford uses it in the F-150 Lightning Standard Range. For daily commuting with home charging, LFP is arguably the more durable, lower-stress chemistry.

Sodium-ion enters as a budget alternative that trades range for extreme cold resilience, low cost, and supply-chain independence. If CATL or competitors bring sodium-ion to the US market post-2026 (likely through non-FEOC joint ventures or licensing), expect it first in entry-level models targeting the $20,000-$28,000 price bracket.

## How Long Do EV Batteries Actually Last?

The fear that EV batteries need frequent, expensive replacement is one of the most persistent myths in the industry. Real-world degradation data tells a more reassuring story.

Typical lithium-ion EV battery degradation (aggregated fleet data):

* Year 1: ~2-5% capacity loss (initial formation loss)
* Years 2-5: ~1-2% per year (linear phase)
* Years 6-10: ~1-1.5% per year (gradual taper)
* At 100,000 miles: Most modern packs retain 88-94% of original capacity
* At 200,000 miles: Typical retention is 80-88%, depending on chemistry and usage

Data from Geotab's fleet study of over 10,000 EVs shows an average annual degradation rate of approximately 2.3% across all chemistries and conditions — meaning the average EV battery retains roughly 88% capacity after 5 years. LFP packs in temperate climates with moderate charging habits often exceed 90% retention at the 5-year mark.

The critical insight: most EV batteries will outlast the vehicle itself. A 2026 EV with a 300-mile EPA range and 85% capacity retention at year 10 still delivers ~255 usable miles — more than adequate for the vast majority of drivers. Complete battery failure (sudden, catastrophic loss) is extremely rare in modern packs with active thermal management.

## Battery Warranty Terms: What's Actually Covered

Federal law mandates that EV battery warranties cover a minimum of 8 years or 100,000 miles (whichever comes first) in most states, and 10 years/150,000 miles in California Air Resources Board (CARB) states including California, New York, Massachusetts, and others. Here's how major manufacturers structure their coverage in 2026:

| Manufacturer | Warranty Term | Capacity Threshold | Coverage Details |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Tesla (Model 3/Y LFP) | 8 yr / 100,000 mi | 70% retention | Defects + excessive degradation below threshold |
| Tesla (Model S/X NMC) | 8 yr / 150,000 mi | 70% retention | Defects + excessive degradation below threshold |
| Hyundai/Kia | 10 yr / 100,000 mi | 70% retention | Defects + degradation; transferable to 2nd owner (reduced term) |
| Ford | 8 yr / 100,000 mi | 70% retention | Defects + excessive degradation |
| GM (Ultium platform) | 8 yr / 100,000 mi | 70% retention | Defects + capacity loss below threshold |
| BMW | 8 yr / 100,000 mi | 70% retention | Defects + degradation; some models offer 8yr/125,000 mi |
| Rivian | 8 yr / 175,000 mi | 70% retention | Defects + excessive degradation |

What the warranty covers: Manufacturing defects, cell failures, and capacity degradation that falls below the stated threshold (typically 70% of original capacity). If your 80 kWh pack drops below 56 kWh usable capacity within the warranty period, the manufacturer must repair or replace it at no cost.

What it doesn't cover: Damage from accidents, flooding, improper modifications, or use outside manufacturer guidelines (e.g., persistent 100% SoC storage on NMC packs if the manual advises against it). Normal gradual degradation above the 70% threshold is considered expected wear and is not warrantable.

## EV Battery Replacement Costs: The Real Numbers

Out-of-warranty battery replacement is the scenario that generates the most anxiety. Here's what it actually costs in 2026, based on manufacturer service data and independent repair shop estimates:

| Vehicle / Pack Size | Chemistry | Replacement Cost (parts + labor) | Typical Replacement Timeline |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Tesla Model 3 Std Range (60 kWh) | LFP | $12,000 – $15,000 | Rarely needed within 15+ years |
| Tesla Model Y Long Range (75-82 kWh) | NMC | $14,000 – $18,000 | Rarely needed within 12-15 years |
| Hyundai Ioniq 5 (77.4 kWh) | NMC | $13,000 – $17,000 | Rarely needed within 12-15 years |
| Ford F-150 Lightning Ext Range (131 kWh) | NMC | $20,000 – $28,000 | Rarely needed within 12-15 years |
| Chevrolet Bolt EV (65 kWh) | NMC | $10,000 – $14,000 | Recall-replaced packs; otherwise 15+ years |
| Nissan LEAF (40-62 kWh) | NMC (passive cooling) | $8,000 – $12,000 | Earlier degradation possible; 10-12 years |

Context that matters: Pack-level battery prices have fallen from over $1,000/kWh in 2010 to roughly $80-$145/kWh in 2026, depending on chemistry. BloombergNEF's 2025 battery price survey confirms this downward trajectory, and sodium-ion cells are expected to push pack prices below $60/kWh at scale — which would bring a 60 kWh replacement pack below $5,000 in parts cost alone.

Additionally, module-level repair is increasingly viable. Many modern packs (including GM's Ultium and Hyundai's E-GMP platform) allow individual module replacement rather than full-pack swaps, reducing out-of-warranty repair costs by 40-60%. A single failed module might cost $1,500-$3,000 to replace versus $15,000+ for a complete pack.

## Factors That Affect EV Battery Life — and How to Maximize It

Battery degradation is inevitable but highly variable. The same pack can lose 8% or 18% over five years depending on how it's treated. Here are the primary factors and evidence-based strategies to slow degradation:

1. State of Charge (SoC) habits:

* NMC packs: Avoid sustained storage at 100% or below 10%. Daily charging to 80-90% is optimal. Charge to 100% only before long trips and drive off promptly.
* LFP packs: Tesla and Ford recommend periodic 100% charges (weekly or bi-weekly) because LFP's flat voltage curve makes SoC estimation inaccurate without full-calibration cycles. Daily 100% is more acceptable on LFP than on NMC.
* Sodium-ion (future): Early CATL guidance suggests LFP-like behavior — less sensitivity to high SoC, but long-term data is still accumulating.

2. Fast-charging frequency:

* DC fast charging (50-350 kW) generates significant heat. Occasional use (road trips, 1-2 times per week) has minimal impact. Daily DC fast charging, especially without preconditioning, accelerates degradation by an estimated 1-3% per year versus Level 2 home charging.
* Always use battery preconditioning when navigating to a fast charger — most modern EVs do this automatically when a Supercharger or DC station is set as your navigation destination.

3. Temperature extremes:

* Sustained exposure to ambient temperatures above 95°F (35°C) accelerates electrolyte decomposition. Garage parking in hot climates measurably extends pack life.
* Extreme cold doesn't cause permanent damage but temporarily reduces available capacity. Charging in sub-freezing temperatures without preconditioning can cause lithium plating on NMC anodes — a permanent degradation mechanism. Most EVs block or severely limit DC fast charging below 32°F until the pack warms.

4. Depth of discharge:

* Shallow cycles (e.g., 40-80%) are gentler than deep cycles (5-100%). You don't need to obsess over this — modern BMS systems manage it automatically — but avoiding frequent 0% events (running the pack completely dead) is wise.

## How to Check and Monitor Your Battery's State of Health (SoH)

State of Health (SoH) is the percentage of your battery's original usable capacity that remains available. A new 75 kWh pack at 92% SoH effectively holds ~69 kWh. Here's how to monitor it:

* In-vehicle displays: Some EVs (notably the Nissan LEAF with its 12-bar capacity gauge, and Tesla via the service menu) show degradation indicators. Tesla owners can access SoH data through the hidden service mode or via the TeslaFi/third-party apps that read vehicle telemetry.
* OBD-II diagnostic tools: Devices like the OBDLink MX+ paired with apps such as LeafSpy (Nissan), ABRP (generic), or Tesla-specific tools can read the BMS-reported SoH figure directly.
* Dealer diagnostic reports: Request a battery health check during scheduled service. Most manufacturers can print a SoH report showing current vs. original capacity.
* Manual calculation: Track your kWh used per full charge cycle. If your 77.4 kWh pack (Hyundai Ioniq 5) originally accepted 74 kWh from 5-100% and now accepts only 66 kWh, your SoH is roughly 89%.
* Range tracking: Compare your current EPA-equivalent range (miles per kWh × current usable kWh) to the original sticker. A consistent 10% range drop over 3 years with similar driving conditions suggests ~10% degradation — though seasonal temperature effects must be factored out.

## Emerging Battery Tech: Solid-State, Silicon Anode, and What's Next

Beyond sodium-ion, several next-generation technologies are in development. Here's a realistic, no-hype assessment of their timelines:

* Solid-state batteries: Toyota, Samsung SDI, and QuantumScape are targeting limited production between 2027-2030. Solid-state cells promise 350-500 Wh/kg energy density (potentially 500+ mile EVs) and faster charging. However, manufacturing cost and yield challenges remain unsolved at scale. Expect initial deployment in premium, low-volume vehicles — not mainstream models — before 2030. Not currently available in any production EV.
* Silicon-dominant anodes: Companies like Sila Nanotechnologies and Group14 are replacing graphite anodes with silicon composites, boosting energy density by 20-40%. Mercedes-Benz's G-Class electric (2025+) uses silicon-anode cells from Sila. Expect broader adoption by 2027-2028 as production scales. Limited availability now; expanding.
* Lithium manganese iron phosphate (LMFP): An evolution of LFP adding manganese for ~15-20% higher energy density while retaining LFP's cost and safety advantages. CATL and Gotion are shipping LMFP cells in 2025-2026. Expect LMFP to become the dominant "standard-range" chemistry by 2028-2029. Entering production now.
* Sodium-ion (2nd generation): CATL has stated it aims for 200 Wh/kg in Gen-2 sodium-ion cells, which would make the chemistry viable for mid-range vehicles (250-300 mile EPA). Timeline: 2027-2029 at earliest. Announced; not yet in production.

For buyers in 2026, these technologies are context — not purchasing factors. Today's LFP and NMC packs are mature, well-understood, and backed by comprehensive warranties. The best battery is the one that matches your driving pattern, climate, and budget right now.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How long do EV batteries last in years and miles?

Modern liquid-cooled EV batteries (LFP and NMC) typically retain 80-90% capacity after 10 years or 150,000-200,000 miles under normal use. Most packs will functionally outlast the vehicle they're installed in. The 8-year/100,000-mile federal warranty minimum provides a strong baseline; many packs exceed this by a wide margin.

### How much does it cost to replace an EV battery?

Full pack replacement costs range from approximately $8,000 for a smaller pack (Nissan LEAF, 40 kWh) to $28,000 for the largest packs (Ford F-150 Lightning Extended Range, 131 kWh). Most common mid-size packs (60-80 kWh) fall in the $12,000-$18,000 range including labor. However, replacement is rarely needed — the vast majority of EVs are retired or sold before the pack fails. Module-level repairs can reduce costs by 40-60%.

### What does the EV battery warranty cover?

Manufacturer battery warranties cover defects and capacity degradation below a specified threshold — typically 70% of original capacity — for 8 years/100,000 miles (or 10 years/100,000-150,000 miles in CARB states and for certain brands). If your battery drops below the threshold within the warranty period, the manufacturer replaces or repairs it at no cost. Warranties do not cover accident damage, misuse, or normal gradual degradation above the threshold.

### How do I check and maximize my EV battery health?

Monitor SoH through your vehicle's service menu, OBD-II diagnostic tools, dealer health reports, or by tracking kWh accepted per charge cycle. To maximize longevity: charge NMC packs to 80-90% daily (100% only for trips), charge LFP packs to 100% periodically for calibration, minimize daily DC fast charging, precondition before fast charging, avoid sustained storage at extreme SoC levels, and garage-park in hot climates.

### LFP vs NMC — which battery chemistry is better for me?

Choose NMC if you need maximum range (300+ miles EPA) in a larger or performance-oriented vehicle, and you're willing to manage SoC more carefully (avoiding sustained 100%). Choose LFP if you prioritize longevity, lower cost, thermal safety, and daily-driver convenience (regular 100% charging is acceptable). For most commuters with home charging and daily drives under 60 miles, LFP is the lower-stress, longer-lasting option. NMC remains necessary for long-range and towing applications.

### Will CATL sodium-ion batteries be available in US EVs in 2026?

Not in any meaningful volume. CATL's sodium-ion packs are entering Chinese-market budget EVs in 2026, but US availability is blocked by FEOC sourcing rules under IRS §30D clean vehicle credit requirements. If sodium-ion reaches the US market, it will likely be through non-CATL manufacturers or licensed production — and not before 2028 at the earliest.

Contemporary Amperex Technology Co., Ltd. (CATL) plans to begin large-scale deployment of its sodium-ion batteries across multiple fields in 2026. The company disclosed the roadmap at its supplier conference in Ningde, Fujian province, on December 28, signaling that its sodium-ion cells are commercially ready for battery-swap networks, passenger cars, commercial vehicles, and energy storage systems.

CATL outlined a “dual-star” strategy, under which sodium-ion and lithium-ion battery technologies will be developed in parallel. Industry observers note that the global sodium-ion battery sector is shifting from early-stage commercialization toward widespread adoption. So far, such batteries have mainly been used in energy storage projects, short-range electric vehicles, and auxiliary power applications. With average cell prices in 2025 staying significantly below those of lithium-ion batteries, strong market growth is forecast through 2030.

In April 2025, CATL introduced its Naxtra sodium-ion brand and started mass production of cells capable of operating between –40°C and 70°C. Its initial offerings include modular power batteries for passenger vehicles and a 24-volt integrated battery pack for heavy trucks, representing CATL’s first commercial sodium-ion product series.

Over the past year, CATL has also reported key technical advances. In September 2025, the company confirmed that its next-generation sodium-ion battery can enable a pure-electric driving range of over 500 kilometers in passenger cars, with mass production set to begin in 2026. The cell delivers an energy density of up to 175 Wh/kg and has already met China’s latest national safety standard for EV traction batteries (GB 38031-2025).

CATL’s sodium-ion products were the first to obtain certification under this new standard, which will take effect in mid-2026 and sets strict requirements for thermal stability, mechanical impact resistance, and fast-charge endurance. Independent tests have verified full compliance with all safety regulations.

The company highlights that sodium-ion chemistry offers improved safety and better low-temperature performance compared with conventional lithium-ion batteries, effectively addressing challenges in cold climates. Moreover, these batteries help extend driving range, cut carbon emissions, and reduce reliance on lithium resources. CATL’s 2026 deployment plan aligns with China’s national strategies for energy storage and new-energy vehicles, which are supported by policies and industry efforts to promote alternative battery technologies.

# CATL unveils world’s first mass-production sodium-ion battery for commercial vehicles

**2 min to read**

Jan 22, 2026 10:43 AM CET

Liu Miao

4

Tianxing II, the industry's first mass-produced sodium-ion battery. Credit: Auto Black Tech on Weibo

Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. Limited (CATL), world’s battery manufacturing giant, officially unveiled its Tianxing II light commercial vehicle battery series on January 22, 2026. The highlight of the launch is the low-temperature version, which represents the industry’s first mass-produced sodium-ion battery.

The 45 kWh sodium-ion battery boasts an energy density of 175Wh/kg and a cycle life exceeding 10,000 cycles. It is the world’s first battery to receive certification under the new GB 38031-2025 national standard and is designed to power small and micro vans and light trucks.

Compared to lithium batteries, this battery has exceptional cold-weather performance. In extreme temperatures as low as -40°C, the battery maintains 90% of its usable capacity. Moreover, it allows for immediate charging even when completely frozen at -30°C, eliminating the winter operation challenges faced by commercial vehicles in cold regions.

There will be four versions of the Tianxing II battery: Low-Temperature (sodium-ion), Fast-Charging, Long-Range and High-Temperature Fast-Charging.

Sodium is over 1,000 times more abundant in the earth’s crust than lithium, with extraction costs at merely 1/20 of lithium. This cost advantage is expected to reduce battery costs and improve the economic feasibility of light commercial electric vehicles in the long term.

Beyond the low-temperature sodium-ion version, the Tianxing II series includes three additional variants (lithium-ion type):

The Fast-Charging Version features high-rate charging technology that powers the battery from 20% to 80% in 18 minutes. For standard 100 kWh electric vehicles, a single fast charge can add approximately 150 kilometers of range.

The Long-Range Version sets a new record for light commercial vehicles with a single-pack capacity of 253 kWh, achieving a maximum range of 800km. This variant is designed primarily for long-distance logistics between cities. When paired with CATL’s Taishan pack architecture, it reduces vehicle weight by approximately 260kg compared to batteries with equivalent capacity, increasing effective payload while reducing energy consumption.

The High-Temperature Fast-Charging Version targets last-mile delivery and self-owned vehicle operations, particularly in southern high-temperature regions. Equipped with a customized liquid cooling thermal management system, it maintains stable fast-charging performance and battery life in high-temperature environments. This version balances high reliability with low operating costs, making it suitable for short-distance, high-frequency light commercial scenarios such as supermarket deliveries and community distribution.

Tianxing is a battery brand for commercial vehicles, launched by CATL in July 2024.

# CATL confirms 2026 large-scale sodium-ion battery deployment in multiple sectors

**3 min to read**

Dec 28, 2025 5:03 PM CET

Adrian Leung

9

CATL outlines multi-sector use cases for sodium-ion battery technology. Credit: CarNewsChina

Contemporary Amperex Technology Co., Ltd. (CATL) said at its supplier conference in Ningde, Fujian province, on December 28, 2025, that it plans to deploy its sodium-ion battery technology at scale across multiple sectors in 2026, according to IT-home. The company described expanded applications in battery swap systems, passenger vehicles, commercial vehicles, and energy storage, indicating a significant commercial deployment phase for sodium-ion technology next year.

Chinese financial media, Sina, reported that at the supplier conference, CATL said its sodium-ion and lithium-ion battery technologies are expected to develop in parallel, describing this as a “dual-star” trend with broader deployment in 2026. Analysts said the global sodium-ion battery industry is shifting from early commercialization toward scaled deployment, with current market use concentrated in energy storage, low-range vehicles, and auxiliary systems, and anticipated expansion into passenger and commercial vehicles. Those reports noted that, in 2025, average sodium-ion cell prices remained significantly lower than those of lithium-ion equivalents, and industry forecasts project substantial growth in the sodium-ion market through 2030.

In April 2025, CATL announced the launch of its sodium-ion battery brand, Naxtra, and stated that large-scale production of sodium-ion cells had begun. These products are designed to operate across a wide temperature range from -40 °C to 70°C. They are offered in both passenger-vehicle power-battery formats and a 24V integrated battery solution for heavy trucks. The product line was introduced as the company’s first commercially oriented series of sodium-ion cells.

Earlier disclosures by CATL have provided additional technical context for its sodium-ion battery roadmap. In September 2025, the company said its next-generation sodium-ion battery supports a pure-electric driving range of more than 500 kilometers in passenger-vehicle applications and is ready for mass production, aligned with a 2026 timeline. CATL stated that the battery achieves an energy density of up to 175 Wh/kg and has passed China’s latest national safety standard for electric-vehicle traction batteries, with large-scale supply expected to proceed in line with customer rollout schedules.

The company’s sodium-ion battery products have passed China’s latest national battery standard, GB 38031-2025, for electric vehicle traction batteries, making them the first sodium-ion batteries to achieve this certification. The national standard, scheduled to take effect in mid-2026, sets stringent safety requirements for thermal stability, mechanical impact resistance, and fast-charge cycling performance. Third-party testing showed that CATL’s sodium-ion cells and battery packs met all required safety tests under the new standard.

CATL has also highlighted performance features of its sodium-ion batteries, noting their improved safety profile compared with traditional lithium-ion chemistries and performance advantages in low-temperature conditions, which the company says could address performance limitations in extreme cold regions. Sodium-ion cells have been reported to achieve energy densities that support extended pure-electric driving range in passenger-vehicle applications, while enabling lower carbon emissions and reduced reliance on lithium resources.

The development of sodium-ion technology has progressed alongside broader national energy storage and new energy vehicle strategies in China, with related policies and industrial plans supporting research, certification, and deployment of alternative battery chemistries. CATL’s planned 2026 rollout of sodium-ion batteries aligns with the broader effort to advance battery technologies for diverse applications.
